extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and activists interested in media freedom and censorship in Bangladesh
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the laws, practices, and grounds used by state and state-linked actors to censor speech, media, film, books, and the internet in Bangladesh. Includes legal provisions, technical measures, examples of blocked material, and reported tactics against journalists and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 39 constitutional protection with restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 39 of the constitution of Bangladesh protects free speech subject to certain restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech is constitutionally protected but the protection is qualified by unspecified statutory or administrative restrictions; this constitutional clause is repeatedly invoked in discussions of censorship and legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital Security Act (DSA) as tool to suppress speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Digital Security Act has been criticized as a tool to suppress the press; it penalizes journalists for obtaining information, documents, and pictures from government offices without government authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported effects include a chilling effect on free speech and investigative journalism, the ability to arrest journalists without warrants, restrictions on bail, and over a thousand cases filed under the Act (Amnesty International called it 'draconian'). Examples: arrests and prosecutions of journalists under the DSA; high-profile cases cited in press coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast Act 2018 restrictions on broadcast media
rubrics_metrics.description: The Broadcast Act 2018 is designed to regulate broadcast media and allows the arrest of journalists without warrants and restricts bail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law is described as aimed at cracking down on television talk shows and other broadcast criticism; cited as creating legal risk for broadcasters and contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: NTMC content blocking and filtering system
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC) can block content critical of the government via a 'Content Blocking and Filtering System' and monitors electronic communication in Bangladesh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NTMC is presented as a central technical actor able to block websites and filter content across networks; cited in connection with blocking news sites and online surveillance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval and use of deep packet inspection (DPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has approved the use of deep packet inspection to monitor web traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DPI is cited as a technical capability used to inspect and potentially block or throttle online traffic; mentioned alongside other surveillance measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use or suspected use of Pegasus spyware
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2021 the Bangladeshi government was suspected to have used Pegasus spyware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pegasus is listed as an example of intrusive surveillance software suspected to be used against critics and journalists; used to illustrate advanced surveillance capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking and throttling of internet and social media
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has throttled internet speed (e.g., during 2018 road-safety protests) and blocked social media or websites (YouTube, Facebook, news sites) at various times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocking has been applied for reasons ranging from 'critical of government' content to alleged concerns about religious offense or piracy; examples include multi-day social media blocks in 2015 and ad hoc blocks of news sites such as The Daily Star, The Wire, Swedish Radio, Al Jazeera, Netra news, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumvention of formal procedure by intelligence agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites have been blocked by intelligence agencies circumventing the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) and proper procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: blocking of Joban and others reportedly done by intelligence agencies rather than following BTRC protocols; indicates extra-legal or opaque blocking mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pornography campaign used to ban websites
rubrics_metrics.description: An anti-pornography campaign resulted in banning 20,000 websites and blogs; some banned sites were accused of publishing content critical of the government and Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICT Minister Mustafa Jabbar described bans as part of a 'war on pornography'; cited example: somewhereinblog.net (partner of Deutsche Welle) was banned allegedly for criticism despite being a blogging platform that bans explicit content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds used by film censor board (political/sensitive/provocative content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bangladesh Film Censor Board has censored or banned films for being 'anti-nationalistic', satirizing political figures, depicting sensitive army activity, showing names of security forces, depicting 'frightening' scenes, or for specific political symbols (e.g., Mujib Coat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple film examples and bans cited from 1991 onward (Remembrance of '71, Nodir Naam Modhumoti, Muktir Gaan, Nomuna, Hridoy Bhanga Dheu, Mor Thengari, Rana Plaza, Faraaz) illustrating the application of these grounds and occasional later reversal after political changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book bans for blasphemy, hurting religious sentiment, or 'promoting extremism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Books have been banned for blasphemy or for 'hurting the religious sentiment of Muslims' and books by some authors (e.g., Syed Abul Ala Maududi) were removed for allegedly promoting extremism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Taslima Nasreen's Wild Wind and My Girlhood were banned for blasphemy; removal of Maududi's books from mosques and libraries; High Court orders and bans in specific cases (e.g., Diya Arefin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic litigation and criminal cases to intimidate editors/journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: The government and ruling party activists have filed numerous criminal cases and civil claims (e.g., around 80 criminal cases against Mahfuz Anam seeking large damages) to intimidate editors and prevent coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include repeated filings in multiple courts forcing travel for bail, demands for large damages, withdrawal of advertising, and pressure to limit editorial output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest, detention, and prosecution of journalists (including without warrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have been arrested, detained, prosecuted and in some cases sentenced without proper procedure; executive magistrates have detained and sentenced reporters, and arrests under statutes like the DSA have occurred without warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arrests in 2019 and 2020, detention and torture allegations (Ariful Islam case), use of arbitrary or politically motivated charges (murder, terrorism), and lengthy detentions cited by UN special rapporteurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative suspensions of public-sector critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors, government officers, and academics have been suspended for criticizing the government's response to COVID-19 or other policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include suspensions after criticism of pandemic response; cited as part of broader suppression beyond press actors to professional and academic critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling critical reporting as 'rumors' to discredit and suppress
rubrics_metrics.description: Government officials publicly label information critical of the government as 'rumors', using that classification to justify pressure or suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: government responses to Netra news reporting during COVID-19 where ministers warned against 'rumors' and intelligence agents pressured relatives of expatriate editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chilling effect and self-censorship by media outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors report practicing self-censorship, with 50–80% of stories being censored internally to avoid trouble with the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-censorship arises from legal risk (DSA, Broadcast Act), litigation threats, loss of advertising, and fear of reprisals; cited by Human Rights Watch and Reuters reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking or restricting games and other online services
rubrics_metrics.description: Various games (e.g., PUBG Mobile, Free Fire) and other internet services have at times been blocked or unable to offer services in Bangladesh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as part of broader internet restrictions; specific justification or official criteria for these blocks are sometimes unspecified and marked 'citation needed' in the article.
